title: Australia’s Sanctions on West Bank Settlers Increase Pressure
content:
Australia announced on November 18 further targeted sanctions on three individuals and four entities involved in illegal settlement expansion and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the West Bank. Although these sanctions are a welcome step, they are long overdue and don’t go far enough. 

The situation in the West Bank is dire. State-backed settler violence has risen to all-time highs. Tens of thousands of Palestinians have been displaced and 1,394 killed by settlers or soldiers in the West Bank since the start of 2023. The number of illegal Israeli settlements has nearly doubled, including the E1 settlement project, which even Israel’s allies have called a “red line,” and which Israeli ministers openly boast is intended to erase any possibility of a future Palestinian state. 

On the same day as Australia’s announcement, the United Kingdom announced sanctions against eight construction companies and property development firms that have not, until now, been sanctioned by any government. The individuals and companies sanctioned by Australia, however, have previously been sanctioned by the United Kingdom and other states.

title: Australia: Use Vietnam Dialogue to Press for Rights Reforms
content:
(Sydney) – Australian officials should press the Vietnamese government to release political prisoners and reverse its intensifying repression of human rights during the upcoming 21st Australia-Vietnam Human Rights Dialogue, Human Rights Watch said today. The case of an Australian national Tran Hiep, a democracy and human rights activist, is of particular concern. He has been detained in Vietnam since he was reported missing in Cambodia in September 2026. 

Human Rights Watch urged Australia, in a submission to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, to seek clear, concrete, and measurable progress from Vietnam on issues including political prisoners, labor rights, transnational repression, and freedom of religion and belief.

“Since Australia’s last dialogue, Vietnam has sharply intensified human rights abuses both inside and outside the country,” said Daniela Gavshon, Australia director at Human Rights Watch. “Australia needs to make it clear to Vietnam that merely holding another meeting is not itself a measure of progress.”

title: US Tries but Fails to Dilute UN Human Rights Resolutions
content:
The United States has recently made a concerted effort to water down draft resolutions at the United Nations that reference the rights of women and girls, sexual orientation and gender identity, and the International Criminal Court (ICC).

The US efforts at the General Assembly’s Third Committee, which focuses on human rights, highlight the Trump administration’s positioning as an outlier among established democracies as it picks and chooses among universal human rights.

Unlike in the UN Security Council, where the US and the other four permanent members have a veto and the US has successfully struck out language on the ICC, gender, and other topics — no single country can block General Assembly resolutions.

At the Third Committee, the US targeted language in draft resolutions referencing sexual and reproductive rights for women and girls. For resolutions on violence against women and girls and trafficking in women and girls, the US proposed adding “in accordance with national laws” after such references. The proposed amendments reflect the Trump administration’s efforts to dismantle internationally protected reproductive rights.

title: World Court Finds Myanmar Committed Rohingya Genocide
content:
(The Hague) – The International Court of Justice’s (ICJ) landmark ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya is a historic milestone in their long quest for justice, Human Rights Watch said today. On November 19, 2026, the ICJ found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya during the 2016-2017 “clearance operations,” carried out by Myanmar’s military.

In the case brought by Gambia against Myanmar for alleged violations of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (Genocide Convention), the court ruled for Gambia, with a nine to six vote by the judges, that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. This is the first time that the ICJ found a country responsible for committing genocide. The court also found that Myanmar violated other obligations under the Genocide Convention, including the obligations to punish those responsible for genocide and to prevent genocide. The court’s ruling is final and cannot be appealed.

title: ‘Today the Truth Has Been Recognized’
content:
As the International Court of Justice in The Hague delivered its judgment on November 19 in the landmark case that Gambia brought against Myanmar for violating the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, thousands of Rohingya waited anxiously in refugee camps in Bangladesh.  

In the Jamtoli Camp 15 in Cox's Bazar District, many crowded around a television. About two hours into the reading of the judgment, it started to rain. But no one moved.

The court’s president spoke in English, a language rarely heard in the crowded camps where over a million Rohingya sought refuge after fleeing Myanmar military attacks in 2017. At 5:13 p.m. local time, a community leader relayed the court’s ruling in the Rohingya language to the waiting crowd, telling them that, by nine votes to six, the court found Myanmar “committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State.” 

The crowd clapped and cheered; many were in tears.

“The Myanmar military tried to convince the world that we had lied,” said 58-year-old Monajat Alam, from Rathedaung Township. “Today, the truth has been recognized.”

title: World Court Finds Myanmar Responsible for Rohingya Genocide
content:
(The Hague) – The International Court of Justice on November 19, 2026, found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya during the 2016-2017 “clearance operations” carried out by Myanmar’s military, in the case brought by Gambia against Myanmar for alleged violations of the Genocide Convention. The court’s ruling is final and cannot be appealed.

The following quote can be attributed to Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch: 

“The International Court of Justice’s landmark ruling is long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured from Myanmar’s military. The ruling also provides a significant precedent for victims of genocide, and other grave crimes, across the world in their own quest for justice.”

“Myanmar should swiftly comply with the court’s judgment and end its oppression of the Rohingya. Concerned governments should strongly support the Rohingya and promote justice for atrocities, press Myanmar’s junta to comply with the judgment, and ensure the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar.”

title: Sudan: Transfer War Crimes Suspects to ICC
content:
(The Hague) – Sudanese authorities should immediately transfer former Interior Minister Ahmed Haroun to the International Criminal Court (ICC) to face charges in The Hague, Human Rights Watch said today. Haroun was recently taken into Sudanese custody and faces ICC war crimes and crimes against humanity charges, committed in Sudan’s Darfur region, in 2003 and 2004.

On November 8, 2026, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) reportedly re-arrested Haroun, interior minister of Sudan in 2007, when an ICC arrest warrant was issued against him. He was arrested one day after he took part in a video podcast interview, his first public appearance since 2019. The armed forces have not officially confirmed Haroun’s whereabouts, but media reported that he is detained in Khartoum state.

title: Human Rights Watch Mourns Death of Activist Nabeel Rajab
content:
(New York) – Nabeel Rajab, a prominent human rights activist from Bahrain and a close partner of Human Rights Watch, passed away on November 17, 2026, at the age of 62. He reportedly died in Türkiye following a heart attack.

Rajab rose to prominence as a human rights defender in Bahrain in the 1990s, and in 2000 he co-founded the Bahrain Human Rights Society, one of Bahrain’s first human rights organizations. He then co-founded the Bahrain Centre for Human Rights in 2002, later becoming its president, and co-founded and was executive director of the Gulf Centre for Human Rights starting in 2011.

Rajab had served as a member of the Human Rights Watch Middle East and North Africa division’s advisory committee since 2010, playing a key role not only in supporting Human Rights Watch work in Bahrain, but also providing guidance to the documentation and advocacy work that Human Rights Watch carries out across the region.

title: Burkina Faso Targets Critics in Exile
content:
Journalists, activists and political opponents who fled Burkina Faso to escape the junta’s repression now risk arrest and prosecution abroad, as the country’s judicial authorities pursue dozens of individuals over alleged terrorism-related offenses.

Burkina Faso Prosecutor General Désiré Sawadogo announced on November 13 that a special court handling terrorism-related offenses had opened six cases against at least 45 people and entities. All those targeted exposed serious military abuses during counterinsurgency operations and include exiled journalists critical of the junta, among them Ahmed Newton Barry, Issaka Lingani, Inoussa Ouédraogo, Adama Ouedraogo, and Abdoulaye Barry; exiled social media activist Naïm Touré; former foreign affairs minister Alpha Barry, and international journalist Wassim Nasr. They face various charges, including complicity in terrorist associations and financing terrorism.

Burkina Faso sent international arrest warrants and extradition requests to Côte d’Ivoire, France, and the United States, said Sawadogo. He added that Burkina Faso asked the United States to use Meta to identify and prosecute Facebook page administrators accused of promoting terrorism.

title: Cambodia’s Repression Hangs Over Francophonie Summit
content:
As world leaders recently gathered in Phnom Penh to celebrate the 20th Francophonie Summit with the theme of peace and shared prosperity, French President Emmanuel Macron took to the podium to call publicly for an investigation into the killing of former Cambodian lawmaker and French citizen Lim Kimya. It was a rare public rebuke of the Cambodian government by a foreign leader.

A gunman killed Kimya in Bangkok, Thailand in January 2025. Kimya had served as a parliament member with the opposition Cambodia National Rescue Party before its 2017 dissolution.

A Thai court convicted the gunman, Ekkalak Paenoi, in October 2025 and issued arrest warrants for two Cambodian suspects, Ly Ratanakraksmey and Pich Kimsrin, both of whom have connections to high-ranking Cambodian officials. The Cambodian government—like many of its neighbors in Southeast Asia—is increasingly persecuting activists abroad.

The Cambodian government has yet to acknowledge the arrest warrants or start an impartial investigation. Both men remain at large. France has issued Interpol Red Notices for them on charges of complicity in premeditated murder.

title: Rights Defender in Central African Republic Dies
content:
Nicolas Tiangaye, a prominent Central African lawyer, human rights defender, and former prime minister died in Bangui on November 16, at the age of 70. One of the country's most respected rule of law advocates, his career spanned more than four decades.

Tiangaye first came into the spotlight as a young lawyer when he defended the former emperor, Jean-Bédel Bokassa, in 1986. Later he defended the future president, François Bozizé, when he was accused of plotting a coup.

For Tiangaye, the cardinal rule that all defendants must benefit from their right to a fair trial is one he lived by. By the early 1990s, Tiangaye was one of the leading Central African human rights advocates and served as the Bar Association president.

In 1996 he was the lead defense council for Jean-Paul Akayesu before the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. Human Rights Watch strongly advocated for the prosecution of Akayesu hailing his 1998 conviction as a historic international precedent. I once discussed the seminal conviction with Tiangaye and he reiterated that a good lawyer must be willing to defend clients and insist on due process, even in highly charged circumstances.

title: Azerbaijan Jails Parliamentary Watchdog Activists
content:
An Azerbaijani court sentenced two activists affiliated with Meclis.info, an independent platform monitoring the country’s parliament, to lengthy prison terms on dubious financial crime charges on November 12, 2026. These are the latest convictions as part of a wider crackdown that has seen scores of journalists, human rights defenders, and civic activists prosecuted on politically motivated charged since late 2023.

The Baku Grave Crimes Court sentenced Imran Aliyev, Meclis.info’s co-founder, to 10 years in prison, and Elgiz Gahraman, another co-founder and data analyst, to nine years. A third defendant, the platform’s accountant Tamella Musayeva, received a suspended prison sentence. All three were convicted of illegal entrepreneurship, money laundering, currency smuggling, tax evasion, and document forgery.

Launched in 2023, Meclis.info published analyses of Azerbaijan's parliament, scrutinizing lawmakers’ attendance, voting records, and public statements. Aliyev has been in detention since his arrest in April 2024. Gahraman and Musayeva were placed under police supervision in February 2025; Gahraman was taken into custody in the courtroom after the verdict.

title: ICC: Afghanistan Decision Risks Narrowing Access to Justice
content:
(The Hague) – An International Criminal Court (ICC) decision risks hindering a path to justice for victims of grave crimes committed in Afghanistan, Human Rights Watch said today. On November 12, 2026, an ICC pretrial chamber, citing a lack of activity, effectively closed the court’s situation dealing with crimes by US, Afghan government, and other forces prior to the Taliban’s August 2021 takeover.

The ICC prosecutor’s office on November 13 sought to appeal the decision and to seek a stay of the closure decision. Research by Human Rights Watch and others over many years has documented war crimes and crimes against humanity by the Taliban; the Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP), an ISIS-affiliated group; Afghan government forces; and US military and Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) forces.

“Victims of serious international crimes committed by warring parties during Afghanistan’s long conflict have faced many roadblocks to justice,” said Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch. “The ICC judges’ decision threatens to compound barriers to future accountability for US and Afghan government forces.”

title: UN Committee Proposes Drastic Cuts to Afghanistan Investigations
content:
A United Nations budgetary advisory committee has proposed sweeping cuts to the Afghanistan accountability mechanism, established by consensus by the UN Human Rights Council in October 2025 following years of negotiations. 

The Independent Investigative Mechanism for Afghanistan was created to support efforts to hold the Taliban and others responsible for international crimes in Afghanistan to account. It is expected to include a focus on the Taliban’s crimes against humanity of gender persecution. Like similar mechanisms for Myanmar and Syria, it was designed to collect and preserve evidence and prepare files to support criminal prosecutions. Its formation followed years of campaigning by Afghan and international human rights groups on the basis that it could be a key tool in securing justice for victims of grave abuses. Its investigations could also act as a deterrent for current Taliban commanders.

title: Bangladesh: Education Crisis for Rohingya Refugee Children
content:
(Bangkok) – Humanitarian education programs for Rohingya refugee children in Bangladesh are struggling amid a collapse in donor funding, Human Rights Watch said today. Donors should fully fund the education programs, while Bangladesh should recognize and the United Nations should support a separate Rohingya-led school network.

Humanitarian education programs have enrolled 312,000 out of approximately 500,000 school-age Rohingya children in the Bangladesh refugee camps. But the programs, which aid cuts had shuttered for months in 2025, are barely adequate even for the children they reach and may close again, humanitarian officials told Human Rights Watch. While resources are shrinking, about 90,000 more refugee children need schooling this year, due to population growth and new arrivals fleeing atrocities in Myanmar. The donor-supported programs have largely ignored the schools that Rohingya teachers set up in the camps, which are well-regarded by refugees for their quality of education, but lack legal status and reach only about 30,000 students.

title: EU: Countries Plan Rwanda Deportation Centers
content:
(Brussels) – Negotiations to set up an offshore deportation center in Rwanda, which has a shocking human rights record, are a particularly cruel departure from the founding values of the European Union, Human Rights Watch said today.

After months of speculation, Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece, and the Netherlands, alongside Rwanda’s interior minister, confirmed the negotiations on November 16, 2026, on the sidelines of the Vienna Migration Conference organized by the International Centre for Migration Policy Development. The five EU countries confirmed their plan to send people whose asylum claims have been rejected in the EU to Rwanda starting in 2027.

“History has shown that third country transfers violate rights and cause suffering,” said Judith Sunderland, senior associate refugee and migrant rights director at Human Rights Watch. “The choice of a country that has an abysmal human rights record and resists international scrutiny tracks with that history and evokes deep skepticism that any nominal rights safeguards will be respected.”

title: Liberia Lifts a Major Barrier to Education
content:
“Our children are able to go to school again.” That's how one Liberian parent described the impact of a new government policy banning school registration fees for kindergarten through sixth grade. The policy is already helping families who struggled to pay the fees, removing a longstanding barrier to their children's education.

Since the policy took effect in September, Liberian child advocates have interviewed parents in four counties to assess whether schools were complying with the ban. The findings offered encouraging early indications: nearly all 20 parents interviewed knew about the policy and had enrolled their children without paying registration fees.

Parents described the difference the policy was making. “The decision by the ministry is so good,” said a parent in Bong County. “It enables our children to go to school free without worry.” Another parent whose children had previously been out of school said, “For some of us that don’t have money, it helps us a lot.”

title: Armed Groups' Abuses Continue in Border Areas
content:
Since early November, many rural communities in the Catatumbo region, near the Colombia-Venezuela border, have suffered violent abuses and forced displacement as the 33rd Front, a dissident group of the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), has clashed with the National Liberation Army (ELN) over control of the territory.

During a field visit from November 9 to 12, Human Rights Watch interviewed community members, representatives of civil society organizations, humanitarian workers, and local authorities, who said these groups have continued to kill civilians, recruit children, plant antipersonnel mines, carry out drone attacks, and impose strict social control over communities.

People told us that on November 8 in Caño Salado, a rural community in Tibú, members of the 33rd Front threatened residents and accused them of collaborating with the ELN. Two community leaders were killed. “They told people to leave, or they would kill anyone who was involved with the ELN,” a civil society member told Human Rights Watch.

Dozens of families have also been displaced from Bocas de San Miguel and El Diamante, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.

title: Three Years’ Prison in Kyrgyzstan for Alleged Repost
content:
A district court in Bishkek on November 11 sentenced Baktybek Moldaliev, an activist, to three years in jail for allegedly reposting content produced by Kloop Media, which a court had previously declared “extremist”. The case sends a chilling message to social media users across Kyrgyzstan: simply clicking the repost button on a social media platform could land someone in prison.

Moldaliev, 49, who worked as a welder, and commented regularly on politics on Facebook was first detained for a day in November 2025, when police seized his phone as evidence and gained access to it, according to his wife, Elvira Zhusupova.

Six months later in May 2026 Moldaliev was charged with inciting "mass unrest"—vague charges frequently brought against social media users in Kyrgyzstan who are prosecuted for sharing or resharing content online. He was taken into custody where he has remained since. After a month and a half, authorities changed the charges to the production and distribution of extremist materials.

During the November 11 court hearing, Moldaliev denied the allegations, saying that police or other individuals could have used his account to share the content and frame him.

title: Philippine Police Detain Hundreds Protesting Trump Visit
content:
Police in the Philippines arrested and detained at least 245 people protesting the visit of US President Donald Trump to Manila for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit. 

Protests in Manila started on November 15 opposing the Philippine government’s plan to build a technology manufacturing hub in Capas, Tarlac province, under the US government’s “Pax Silica” initiative. The construction will displace hundreds of Indigenous people and small farmers from their homes and farmlands.

An estimated 6,000 people joined the protests despite police efforts to contain demonstrations by banning them everywhere except in “freedom parks” – designated areas where rallies can be held without a permit.

Yet police arrested 236 people on the outskirts of Metro Manila who were traveling from the Southern Tagalog region to the main protest site. Among those detained were 29 farmers including members of the Indigenous Mangyan tribe, 19 journalists, 9 environmental defenders, and 6 human rights workers. Ephraim Cortez of the National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers said 19 children were detained.
